name: Karl Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both your public answer and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground crew for the electricity company in the east side of the city. Most of the cables there are buried, so a day might be pumping water out of a pit on Canal Street, putting up the jointing tent and joining two cable ends by hand for five or six hours. When a fault blows, we dig, find it, cut it out and join it back up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of that, and the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is a clean joint. You strip back the layers, everything lined up, and when it's livened up and holds, you know it was you. Hardest is the money, honestly. I'm still on the lower grade because the full jointer ticket costs a course they keep postponing, and with Leyla's care-home wages we're living pay to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Sounds like most new gadgets I've seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, now can we talk about the grade review. With friends I'd say I'm not surprised; the fault-finding tablet they gave us last year mostly tells us what the old meter told us. I'm not much for posting online, but I'd like a few things that say the hype was overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing changes, and that's a mixed bag for me. The job's safe, but I'm still on the grade below where I should be, and the boiler's held together with tape. Plateau sounds fine if you were already comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep pushing for the jointer course through the union. I'd use the AI thing on my phone now and then like I do now, to explain Deniz's maths homework or tidy up a letter to the manager. Nothing bigger than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by it, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. What was the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I asked it to help me write to the area manager about the postponed course. It made me sound more polite than I felt. Leyla said it was the first letter of mine she didn't have to rewrite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between the lower grade and the full ticket, in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close to three thousand a year. That's the boiler and Mira's school trip and a little left over. It's not life-changing, but it's the difference between counting days to payday and not counting.

S0.say: I'd say good, now can we talk about the grade review, and that the fault-finding tablet mostly told us what the old meter did. Online I'd like a few posts saying the hype was overblown.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changing is a mixed bag: the job is safe, but he's still a grade below where he should be. A plateau sounds fine if you were already comfortable.
S0.do: Keeps working and presses the union for the postponed jointer course worth close to three thousand a year. Uses AI on his phone occasionally for homework help and letters, nothing more.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit bored by it.
S0.quote: Plateau sounds fine if you were already comfortable.
S0.fieldNote: Karl hears the plateau as a reminder of an existing grievance, the postponed grade course. He's matter-of-fact about AI and already uses it lightly for writing. His money pressure is concrete and specific, down to the boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels more like real life to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work straight: if the tasks change, the training has to come with them, paid and on the clock. Down the pub with the lads I'd say the ones who'll get hurt are the young apprentices and the old boys, not people like me in the middle. I'd share union stuff about a just transition, sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think fault-finding changes the most. A program that reads the cable data and points to the exact spot means less digging in the wrong place. That's good, but it's also fewer hours for a crew, and fewer hours for a crew means somebody gets moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new tools have run a few months on another crew, then I'd ask to be on the next round of training. I'd push the union to tie any new kit to the grade review. And I'd try to put twenty a week into a savings pot, because I'd want something there if hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, just that feeling in your stomach when you're down a pit and you smell something you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for another crew to try it first. Why not volunteer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen pilots go wrong. Two years ago they trialled a new joint kit and two of the joints failed in six months, and the crew who tried it took the blame. Let it be proven, then I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, my jointer. He's brilliant with his hands but he can barely type his own timesheet. If the job turns into half screen work, he's going to struggle, and he's got three kids.

S1.say: He'd say training has to come with any change, paid and on the clock, and that apprentices and older workers get hurt most. He'd share union posts about a just transition.
S1.think: He expects AI fault-finding to mean less digging in the wrong place, which is good but means fewer crew hours. Fewer hours means somebody gets moved.
S1.do: Waits a few months for another crew to prove the tools, then asks for the next training round. Pushes the union to tie new kit to the grade review and saves twenty a week.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like smelling something he can't place down a pit.
S1.quote: Two years ago they trialled a new joint kit and two of the joints failed in six months, and the crew who tried it took the blame.
S1.fieldNote: His steadiness is earned from experience: he's watched pilots fail and crews get blamed. He sees himself as safer than apprentices and older workers, and worries about a colleague who struggles with screens. He would adopt the new tools once proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's... two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of things like the grid and a proper safety net, and I'd say it everywhere. At work I'd be at the union office the first day asking what the plan is. Online I'd actually start posting, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. Two years isn't enough time for anything I know how to do. A robot that can join cable in a pit sounds far-fetched to me today, but if you're telling me it's there, then a man on the lower grade with no savings is the one they don't keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: the phone contracts, takeaways, Mira's swimming, sadly. I'd talk to the bank about stretching the mortgage before anything goes wrong. I'd be at union meetings pushing for a redundancy deal and I'd sign up for whatever government support exists, because we'd need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot in a pit sounds far-fetched. Do you believe it, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I've seen what one bad joint does to a street. If they get it right, then fine, it's real. But I'd still want a human standing there for a good while, and I'd say that at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leyla that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll manage, which is what I always say. She'd look at me because she knows that's what I say. Then we'd get the bills out on the kitchen table and go through them one by one.

S2.say: He'd say this is why the grid needs public ownership and a proper safety net, and be at the union office on day one. He'd start posting online, which he never does.
S2.think: Privately he'd be frightened: two years isn't enough for anything he knows how to do, and a lower-grade worker with no savings is the one they don't keep.
S2.do: Cuts phone contracts, takeaways and his daughter's swimming at once and asks the bank about stretching the mortgage. Pushes the union for a redundancy deal and signs up for any government support.
S2.feel: Like the floor's gone, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd tell her we'll manage, which is what I always say. She'd look at me because she knows that's what I say.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline overwhelms his usual wait-and-prove approach. He doubts robots could do jointing safely but accepts the premise reluctantly. His instinct is still collective and public: unions, state support, ownership of the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to fight for a proper plan, and I'd be saying it at union meetings and to anyone at the school gate who'd listen. I'd want something like a transition fund paid for by the companies making the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough time to watch it coming. I'd see the first robot trials on another district, and by then I'd know whether it actually works. That's how I like it, to be honest. Seeing it before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the protection and control course at the technical college, two evenings a week, once I saw a couple of the lads doing it. That's the substation side, setting up the relays that trip when there's a fault, and someone has to set up and check the systems the robots plug into. I'd save what I could and push the union for paid study leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes, but I'd have my hands on something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nothing you know would help in two years. Why would a course help in five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in five years you can finish the course and get a couple of years of practice before it's all robots. In two you'd just be halfway through when the doors close. Same course, different ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay for evening classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe. We've got two, and Leyla's care home is on the bus route. That's about a hundred and twenty a month in insurance and petrol we'd save.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to fight for a proper plan, like a transition fund paid for by the companies making the robots. He'd say it at union meetings and the school gate.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him watch the first robot trials on another district before moving, which is exactly how he likes to change.
S3.do: Signs up for a two-evening protection and control course at the technical college once colleagues do. Sells the second car to save about a hundred and twenty a month and pushes the union for paid study leave.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with his hands on something, which helps.
S3.quote: In two you'd just be halfway through when the doors close. Same course, different ending.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits his style exactly: he can watch others go first, then commit. He picks a related hands-on technical path rather than leaving the trade. The car sale shows he'd pay for change with real cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Deniz would be twenty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse, a decade is long enough for governments and companies to get it right. I'd be pushing that at union meetings and voting for whoever had an actual plan. I'd say it to my kids' teachers too, because they're the ones getting them ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the decade worries me more for my kids than for me. I'll be fifty-three and maybe I'll have something. But Deniz and Mira would come out of school into a world where the robots are arriving, and I don't know what to tell them to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the protection course over three or four years instead of rushing it. I'd sit down with Deniz about what he wants and look at apprenticeships that would still matter. I'd vote and campaign for a transition fund, and keep on with the twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a slower way. It's the kids' faces I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Deniz to study, if he asked tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something with people, like nursing, which is what his mum does in a way. Or electrical, because whatever happens, somebody's got to plug all this in. Then I'd tell him I don't really know, which is the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the government and companies need a plan. If they don't use the ten years, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'll have wasted the one gift we had, which was time. I've seen councils sit on a report for ten years. I'd be angry but not surprised.

S4.say: He'd say a decade leaves no excuse for governments and companies not to get it right, and vote for whoever has a real plan. He'd raise it with his kids' teachers too.
S4.think: He worries more for his children than himself: they'd leave school as the robots arrive, and he doesn't know what to tell them to study.
S4.do: Takes the protection course over three or four years and talks with his son about apprenticeships that would still matter. Votes and campaigns for a transition fund and keeps saving twenty a week.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slower way, thinking of his kids' faces.
S4.quote: Then we'll have wasted the one gift we had, which was time. I've seen councils sit on a report for ten years.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline moves his worry from his own job to his children's futures. He's honest that he doesn't know what to advise them. His trust in public institutions is real but tempered by watching councils stall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company paying for the course now, not next year, and a guarantee from the government that if the job goes, the mortgage doesn't go with it the same month. Some kind of support that lasts long enough to retrain properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everybody talks about jobs, but a bad joint can kill somebody. If they put robots in pits, I want a human signing off on every joint for years, and I want that in law.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about jobs, but a bad joint can kill somebody.
portrait: Karl Yilmaz is a 43-year-old underground cable worker on the city's east side, stuck on a lower grade while he waits for a postponed jointer course, with a care-worker partner and two kids. He changes once something is proven and uses AI now and then, mostly for letters and homework. The plateau and steady pictures leave him calm to uneasy and focused on training and pay. The two-year AGI picture frightens him into cuts and union action, while five and ten years let him plan a protection and control course at night. Over the long timeline, his worry moves from himself to his children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough time for anything he knows how to do and a lower-grade worker with no savings is the one they don't keep.
whatWouldHelp: The company paying for his course now, and government support that keeps the mortgage paid long enough to retrain properly.
